# NERVA: Anomaly Detection Model Benchmark (synthetic data)

## 0. Data provenance: read this first

**Every number in this report comes from synthetic telemetry**, generated by
[`services/anomaly-engine/app/evaluation/scenarios.py`](../../services/anomaly-engine/app/evaluation/scenarios.py)
from fixed random seeds. The generator models four services (`auth-service`, `checkout-service`,
`payment-service`, `search-service`) and two fault shapes; it is the generator's own assumption of what such
telemetry looks like, **not measurements from the cluster**. `auth-service` and `search-service` exist only in
this generator.

What this report **does** show: on identical, labelled data with a strict train / tune / held-out split, how the
four detector designs compare with each other.

What it **does not** show: how a detector performs on real traffic. That evidence is the live drills on the kind
cluster ([LIVE_DRILLS_2026-10-20.md](LIVE_DRILLS_2026-10-20.md)) and the real-capture evaluation in
[`docs/evidence/m2`](m2).

Reproduce exactly (same seeds give the same output on any machine):

```powershell
cd services/anomaly-engine
python -m app.evaluation.compare      # --train-seed 1500 --tune-seed 1000 --eval-seed 2000 are the defaults
```

The numbers below were re-run and matched on 2026-10-20.

## 1. Method

A strict three-way split, so no choice is made on the data it is scored on:

1. **Training set** (`seed=1500`): 4,598 healthy readings only; each model learns "normal" from these.
2. **Tuning set** (`seed=1000`): 4,617 normal snapshots plus faulty runs; each alert line is chosen here under a
   fixed false-alarm budget (at most 0.2% of normal snapshots).
3. **Held-out set** (`seed=2000`): 4,610 normal snapshots plus faulty runs, used **only** for the final scores.

## 2. Held-out results (synthetic)

| Detector | Type | Precision | Recall | F1 | False alarms (normal snapshots) | Worst detection delay | Missed faulty runs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Z-score per service** *(used by M2)* | Statistical, explainable | **0.988** | **1.000** | **0.994** | **0.04% (2/4610)** | **60 s** | **0** |
| Isolation Forest per service | ML ensemble | 0.988 | 1.000 | 0.994 | 0.11% (5/4610) | 225 s | 0 |
| Isolation Forest pooled | ML, one global model | 0.960 | 0.900 | 0.929 | 0.11% (5/4610) | 330 s | 8 |
| Static threshold baseline | Fixed rules | 0.955 | 0.800 | 0.871 | 0.13% (6/4610) | 45 s | 16 (all traffic spikes) |

## 3. Findings, within the limits of synthetic data

1. **Fewer false alarms.** The per-service z-score raised 2 false alarms in 4,610 normal snapshots, against 5
   for Isolation Forest. For a system that proposes real actions, false alarms are the costlier error.
2. **Faster worst-case detection than the forests** (60 s against 225 s and 330 s). The static baseline is
   faster still (45 s) but misses 40% of traffic spikes.
3. **Per-service models beat one pooled model.** The pooled forest missed 8 faulty runs: one "normal" for very
   different services hides faults.
4. **Explainability.** A z-score alert names the metric and its distance from that service's own healthy
   behaviour ("latency_p95_ms is 10.5 usual deviations from normal"), which an operator approving an action can
   check.

## 4. What this means for the deployed system

* `payment-service` is scored by the per-service z-score, with a reference trained on **real** captured healthy
  telemetry (`services/anomaly-engine/app/reference.py`).
* A service without a trained reference falls back to the **static threshold baseline**, the weakest detector
  here on traffic spikes. `checkout-service` uses its own trained reference too; see
  [LIVE_DRILLS_2026-10-20.md](LIVE_DRILLS_2026-10-20.md) for how it was captured and checked.
